lesson.title: Poisoning the Phone Book: DNS Cache Poisoning
lesson.summary: DNS cache poisoning injects a forged record into a resolver's cache, so every client that trusts that resolver is silently redirected to an attacker controlled address until the bad entry expires or is corrected.
lesson.body:
DNS caching exists so that a resolver does not have to contact an authoritative server every single time a client asks for the same domain. Once the resolver gets an answer, it stores that answer for the record's time to live, and hands the cached answer to any client that asks again during that window. This is a genuine performance win, but it also means that whatever the resolver has cached is what every one of its clients will believe, without checking again.

DNS cache poisoning is the act of getting a false record into that cache so that future lookups return a malicious IP address instead of the real one. This is where the local versus shared scope really matters. ARP spoofing only affects devices on the same local network as the attacker. DNS cache poisoning is different in reach: if the poisoned resolver is a shared one, such as an internet provider's recursive resolver or a company's internal DNS server, then every client that queries that resolver inherits the forged record, potentially affecting a large population of unrelated users who have no connection to the attacker's own network.

The classic mechanism behind this attack targets the moment a resolver has no cached answer and has to ask an authoritative server directly. The resolver sends its query and then waits, matching the eventual reply by a transaction identifier along with the source and destination ports and addresses involved. If an attacker can guess or otherwise obtain that transaction identifier and source port quickly enough, the attacker can send a forged reply that appears to come from the authoritative server, racing to arrive before the real answer does. If the resolver accepts the forged reply as legitimate, exactly as a device accepts an unsolicited ARP reply, it caches the attacker's fake record as if it were genuine. This is again a spoofing attack at its core: forging the identity of the authoritative server, exploiting a protocol that was never built to strongly verify who actually sent a given answer.

The practical impact can be serious precisely because DNS lookups are invisible to the end user. If a resolver's cache holds a poisoned record for a banking domain, a user who types that domain into their browser is sent straight to the attacker's server without any obvious warning sign, since nothing about the request itself looked wrong. Notice the contrast with the previous chapter: ARP spoofing requires the attacker to be physically present on the victim's local network and lets the attacker intercept traffic in transit, while DNS cache poisoning requires no local presence at all once the cache is poisoned, and instead sends the victim's connection directly to a server the attacker controls, anywhere on the internet. Both attacks exploit the same underlying weakness, a protocol step that trusts a reply without adequately verifying where it truly came from, just at different layers and different scales.
